title: Delhi Police Tells Supreme Court No Excessive Force Used Against Student Protesters
excerpt: In its counter-affidavit, Delhi Police called the July 20 Sansad Chalo march 'illegal' and said 5,000 officers managed a crowd of over 30,000 amid stone-pelting by 'miscreants.'
body:
• Delhi Police filed a counter-affidavit in the Supreme Court denying excessive force during the July 20 Sansad Chalo march, calling the protest 'illegal' and saying 5,000 officers managed over 30,000 demonstrators.
  • The Supreme Court has ordered preservation of all CCTV footage and digital evidence, barred coercive action against students, and is considering constituting a Special Investigation Team (SIT) for an independent probe.
  • An IIT Patna student has filed an intervention application alleging that police used lathis fitted with nails, pellet guns, and electrified barricades, and that plain-clothes personnel without identification badges participated in the crackdown.
  • The Centre has committed to amnesty for student protesters, and the SC has clarified that states may withdraw FIRs against those without criminal antecedents.

Delhi Police's Defense

Delhi Police has told the Supreme Court that no excessive force was used against student protesters during the July 20 Sansad Chalo march, filing a counter-affidavit that called the march to Parliament "illegal" and defended the police response as proportionate crowd management.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2089594266855293132

The police said approximately 5,000 officers were deployed to manage a crowd that swelled beyond 30,000 protesters, and attributed violence at the scene to "miscreants" rather than students. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the Union government, supported this position, telling the court that students would not typically engage in violence against police officials and suggesting other elements were involved.

What Happened on July 20

The Sansad Chalo march was organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a student-led movement that emerged from widespread anger over alleged paper leaks in the NEET-UG 2026 medical entrance examination. Thousands of students marched from Jantar Mantar toward Parliament demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Police and Rapid Action Force personnel used lathis and tear gas to disperse the crowds as they moved toward Parliament. Multiple media reports documented injuries to over 90 protesters. The Delhi High Court, which heard the matter first, directed preservation of all CCTV footage and ordered Delhi Police to file its response.

Allegations of Brutality

Petitioners before the Supreme Court have painted a starkly different picture from the police account. An IIT Patna student, Toshiwa Yadav, filed an intervention application claiming she suffered a deep head laceration requiring stitches after being assaulted by police personnel.

"The presence and participation of unidentified persons in the use of coercive force against citizens raises serious questions of transparency, accountability and institutional responsibility."

— Intervention application filed by IIT Patna student Toshiwa Yadav

Her plea alleges that lathis fitted with nails were used, that women protesters were assaulted, and that an Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police slapped a woman bystander. Media reports also reference the use of pellet guns, electric shock batons, and electrified barricades by police and RAF personnel.

The Supreme Court Bar Association and the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association both issued statements condemning the police action. The SCBA called the force "wholly unacceptable in a democratic society" and noted that its own members were among the injured.

The Court's Response So Far

Chief Justice Surya Kant has taken several interim steps since July 28. The court ordered the release of all arrested protesters under 18 with no criminal records, directed preservation of all electronic evidence, and barred coercive action against students for the time being.

"Whosoever committed excesses, took law in their hands should be taken to task," the CJI said, adding that the court was considering constituting a Special Investigation Team to conduct an independent probe into all allegations — both against police and against protesters accused of violence.

On August 3, the court clarified that states are free to withdraw FIRs filed against student protesters where legally permissible. The Centre reaffirmed its commitment to amnesty for participants in the protests.

What's Next

A PIL filed in the Delhi High Court alleging excessive police force is listed for hearing on September 11. The Supreme Court continues to hear petitions from both sides — student activists seeking accountability for police action, and the government defending its response while pledging to address the underlying exam integrity concerns.

The case has become a focal point for broader questions about the right to protest and proportionate use of force in India — questions that resonate with diaspora families following developments around NEET and competitive examination reforms.
nri_angle: The student protests over NEET exam integrity have drawn international attention and prompted concerns among Indian-Americans about the fairness of competitive examinations that affect families across the diaspora.
